items.title: Raymond Meeks A Common-Place Book
items.content:
In full declaration, as a fan of all parties involved, I hereby cannot deny my overwhelming urge to state that this book, in the canon of Raymond J. Meeks Esq., is hitherto unnecessary, but welcomed nonetheless. It is a compilation of misses, outtakes, and the unloved and weeded-out, minus one image of an alabaster girl with wet hair and maybe one photograph of some farming equipment that have appeared previously. It is not a best of, thankfully, but instead is a venerable tome of what appears, on the outside, to be a torch-passing exercise between two of photography’s finest living photographers, namely the aforementioned Meeks and the eminent photographer John Gossage, both artists who have had a significant imapct on my way of thinking about what is possible with the medium, both of whom, I have a minor aquaintenace.

While pouring over the book last night, after several previous attempts, I came around to the idea that it fostered some very choice offcuts by Meeks, which made my browsing enjoyable and offered enough to make the book worthwhile. Whereas I had been undecided whether it constituted a holistic approach to the material, I do find the cuts significant, even if there is no particular sense of completeness within the overall project.

The book and selection, administered by Gossage, revealed what had remained invisible in the last 10-13 years of Meeks’ output, and I have to admit that some of the adjacent slices of Ciprian Honey Cathedral were more compelling than some of the images in the original book. In fact, the pond-scum green of many of Meeks’ color images within the book had me contemplating bronze statues, algae, and the choices made to use such garish color, which, oddly, and for the sake of shorthand, worked incredibly well in this book and Ciprian Honey Cathedral, having exemplified the deeper pathology of place and relationships as outlined in the original volume.

This reminded me, interestingly, of what I like about both artists: with Gossage’s work, I gravitate toward his monochrome adventures, and I realized that with Meeks, I find his color attempts more alluring at times than his monochrome forays. It makes me want to see more color from the artist. What is worth noting is that there is certainly an echo of Gossage’s vision and technical uses of the camera in some of Meeks’s later volumes, particularly in Geography of Abandonment and The Inhabitants. I think both artists draw from similar waters and a sense of melancholy, though the influence of Gossage on Meeks is well known. What is interesting about John’s edit is that Meeks’s black-and-white work is some of the work I find least Gossage-like, almost as if there were a conscious move to keep the images where overlap might be obvious at bay, instead concentrating on what makes Meeks, Meeks.

Whereas the design of the book feels very much like Gossage, with the choice of typography and bordering images, I do think the work holds its own as Meeks, though at points it does feel like a Gossage exercise more than a Meeks exercise, and I suspect some of that comes from whatever arrangement has been brokered between the members of The Agency/Steidl imprint. One, if paying attention, can’t help but wonder if this concludes the MACK-era of Meeks’ publishing, and one can’t help but want to be a fly on the wall of that conversation, especially given who has published this volume.

It will be curious which way the wind blows on this decision, which might be construed as semi-risky given how slowly Steidl puts out books and, with the recent financial debacle potentially cleared, what it means for this new collaboration between Steidl and the principal artists involved-Frydland, Gossage, and Meeks.

Overall, if you are a fan of Meeks’s work, this is an excellent addendum to have. Whereas there is a feeling of the procedure being a bit gimmicky with the editing of one artist by another, the full declaration of two artists working in a similar vein and with amicable relations makes it feel like it has a place in the canon, but I am hoping that the rest of the 15 alleged volumes that the co-imprint is to publish might take on a varying design flavor lest all the books begin to look like Gossage exercises.

John’s design is interesting, but I cannot say that I feel it works as well with other artists’ works as it does with his own; maybe that is part of the arrangement of the imprint- who knows. It does have the feel of a faux think tank in its online persona, so maybe this cohesive, if questionable, strategy is part of the mix. If you are a deep Meeks head, this is volume for your shelves. If you have not been sold on his work until this point, I might suggest going over Ciprian Honey Cathedral or The Inhabitants first. Either, as a fan, I have little choice but to recomment it for the color work and novelty alone.

 

Raymond Meeks

A Common-Place Book

The Agency/Steidl

items.title: Steven Shearer Working From Life
items.content:
I was fortunate enough to interview Steven Shearer a few years ago for his exhibition at the Brant Foundation. Their publicity team had reached out to ASX, and I was perplexed that they found us, given how most of our reviewing happens predominantly within the realm of photography, with some emphasis on painting and video on the rare occasion. I had to admit that I did not know anything about Steven’s work, but certainly knew of Peter Brant’s foundation, so I opened the press pack and was absolutely blown away by the work and frankly felt a little backward that I had not encountered it previously; for all intents and purposes, the work seems to be right up my street with its themes of metal-adjacent aesthetic, with insider jokes hinting at the juvelnalia of being a metalhead, those incredibly serious-at-the-time beliefs of rebellion and anti-establishment rhetoric becoming something viable in Steven’s work, a subscription to denim and suicidal inclination in contrary pastel. Much of this works itself out in the cultural consciousness by having Judas Priest on trial and the Satanic Panic of Steven and my youth in the 80s. I also come from an art history background and could immediately recognize his skill and his particular use of color, which he associates with the Fauves while also hinting at a love of occult art and symbolism.

Our interview tackles our crossover interests. In retrospect, the questions may have been a little over the top, but in many ways, that is possibly how I got Steven to open up a bit about the cultural and historical imperatives at work in his painting, for which I am still thankful. Regarding a more sober approach to his work, I think it is easy to speak of the cultural stimuli that shaped his themes, but slightly harder to pin down the art-historical context from which his inspiration might be drawn. Recently, I covered the work of Victor Man, another artist at David Zwirner, whose work also alludes to a tradition of painting in which decay, death, and cryptic, enigmatic tendencies are conveyed through subject matter and technical means, much like Shearer’s. Though different in approach, it left me casually browsing through art historical reference points, and I drew from the experience a series of questions as to why the fascination with what some may refer to as a garish palette has cropped up between these works and how the subject matter, enabled by their usage, has given everything a queasy look, in a art world that is not known for celebrating the wild untamed palette of such choices. It led me to look into the work of Symbolist painters as well as the Fauves.

There is an obscure type of saturnalia involved in the works that evoke something both allegorical and unnatural. Odilon Redon’s Cyclops, from the early decades of the twentieth century, was a first port of call for investigation, followed by William Blake’s painting, and finally a nudge towards the Fauves, with an emphasis on Paul Signac’s Portrait of Félix Fénéon, 1890. Though the Fauves are often applied to Shearer, even in self-reference, I find that this work, however adversarial in its technical color choices, extends beyond that group through his deliberate use of miasmatic, haunted, or necrotic subject matter. There is a prismatic mist in the background of much of his work, an evocation of aether that suggests a portal, or a conjuring at hand, less defined by finite shape and direct patterns of light on surface than by atmosphere and garishness. Color, when applied to landscape, however banal, in the case of Kandinsky or Matisse, breeds a feral type of reading. Otherwise bucolic landscapes, when pushed to the brink of recognizability by the pure use of conflated color choice, materialize at the ends of recognizability. When their palette is exaggerated, the base formula creates a chaotic interpretation of something otherwise mostly benign. In Shearer’s work, this can be seen in his portraiture, a conflation of color that pushes the psychological timbre of his subjects into unnatural territory.

What is spectacular about Shearer’s work is his ability to pull the viewer into his world, look for clues and reference points, and manage the inquest with a forensic eye. The carpet from Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining materializes underneath a seated man. A Victorian train carriage emerges as a motif in several works, reminding one of Augustus Egg’s 1862 painting The Traveling Companions, a narrow precursor to Frederick Lord Leighton’s 1895 Pre-Raphaelite painting Flaming June, which no doubt has also influenced Shearer overall. In fact, to suggest that Shearer is an artist caught between Victorian painting and Robert Pickton’s farm would not be an overvalued statement. The beautiful nature of Pre-Raphaelite Victorian painting, mixed with contemporary subject matter and a Fauvist spin, lands the output squarely in the center. With that in mind, Shearer is also a fanatically organized artist. Rafre interviews and meetings with the artist in his Vancouver studio have attested to the environmental orderliness of Shearer’s domain, and that is likely a productive bulwark for the fever inside his head.

Finally, it would be remiss if we did not acknowledge that Shearer is still a product of his times, and his obsessive catalog of people sleeping, vernacular photography, and Internet archiving are well known. In this book, one is given a tantalizing yet effective overview of his reference material in a single small picture within the essays, which shows something like a nearly 20-volume bound reference library full of images that the artist has put together to draw from, a veritable Shearanica of the aforementioned images. It is a tantalizing image when we think of artists like Richter or Hans-Peter Feldmann, who have similar caches of news clippings and Atlas outlines tucked away in their studios. Seeing Shearer’s references, even in a small image, leaves me wanting to see more, and I am forever grateful to know they exist.

About the book itself, the publisher has done an incredible job with the catalog raisonné, though it is not quite that, but serves a similar purpose in showcasing a significant amount of Shearer’s process and the work itself. It feels like no expense has been spared, and it must have been a monumental job handled with aplomb by the team. As mentioned above, I can imagine Shearer’s eye for detail being significant, and to place this book into the world, it would have had to be handled with equal care by the publisher. It is a large volume full of work, but also expansive in its detailing, meaning the source material for production, file-size-wise, must have been significant and would have required a tremendous amount of publisher consistency to safeguard the work. If one side of artbook making rarely gets the requisitie spotlight, it is the publisher, who often goes to pain=staking lengths to make sure artists, galleries, museums, etc are all happy with the finished product and much of this relies on details, but also a strong hand in following the book through the many guides that work with it from file formating to printing to binding and finally distribution=publishers are often unsung heroes and it is worth noting here as such a large-scale book would need expert hands and eyes on the project to get a result like this.

Overall, this is a fascinating study of an artist in full command of their work, whose intricate talent and ability to draw on subculture-tangibly interesting subject matter- while also nodding to art history, produce an enigmatic and intriguing catalog of work with something like a mid-career survey at its heart. I feel that this is a significant book and that all parties have converged ont the project to make it the best it can possibly be. If you are interested in painting, subculture, or art historical extensions, this is designed with you in mind. I don’t personally believe in rating systems, but I can say that a kind of elegance exudes from the work, and I am overjoyed to have it adorn my shelves. GET IT!

 

Steven Shearer

items.title: Raymond Pettibon Nervous Breakdown: Album Covers
items.content:
If you grew up in a certain period, some of your first experiences with counterculture were inspired by the genius cover artwork of albums by various punk bands, notably Black Flag, by what appeared to be a deranged cartoon columnist. I vividly remember ducking in and out of head/record shops in the Midwest growing up in the late 80s and 90s, being confronted with a nun holding a hairy leg with the title “Slip In In,” and later spotting the now-iconic Sonic Youth Goo album cover in the racks, both appearing to have been illustrated by the same lunatic. When I mention the notion of counterculture, it comes with alot of baggage and timeline understanding.

The counterculture of Raymond Pettibon, like his erstwhile compatriots Frank Kozik (RIP), Derek Hess, Coop, and now very distant Nick Bougas, played a role in the 90s understanding of the failures of original 1968 counterculture and what happened during the intervening years. These artists destabilized the original premise of the counterculture movements of the 60s by emphasizing Charles Manson, John Wayne Gacy, Jim Jones, and every bit of the toxic holocaust that the American dream culture would end up inspiring through the rise of consumer culture and neoliberal consciousness. They took the tools of former generations of counterculture and applied them to serial killers, sleaze, and an effective type of apathy to broadcast the doubt of America and its ideological messaging.

The late 80s and 90s were, in my opinion, the last frontier against conformity and sheep-shearing shit grift. Everything was converging, centralizing, with crossovers in culture being predominant and opposition to politics as something of the norm, something we pretend we see today with the uniparty. What made the cultural production of this time different was the level of cynicism that nascent Gen Xers were able to spin within the web of the times. It was inherent in music from AMREP Records, Touch and Go, and SST Records, and spread through bands like Nirvana, The Jesus Lizard, and Cows, and in films by David Lynch, Greg Araki, Larry Clark, and Nick Zedd. Richard Kern, Sonic Youth, Big Black, Black Flag Flipper, and Swans paved the way for a type of anti-culture, anti-heritage viewpoint that discarded the traditional notion of counterculture for something more snide, more self-reflecting, acknowledging that hippies fucking sucked as much as the suits did. Bands like Sonic Youth spread the message, though in a slightly alternative delivery system, by becoming fashionable and undeniable. Their prescient use of artists from Richard Kern to Raymond Pettibon, Gerhard Richter, and Richard Prince now seems overly canny.

With my coming of age in small-town Wisconsin, with very little else to do except play in bands and steal CDs from Best Buy, I became firmly ensconced in underground music and Adam Parfrey books; it is no mistake that I gravitated toward album cover artwork and found my ability to decipher culture through the iconoclastic works that adorned them. Much of the sentiment and attitude I have carried with me well into my 40s. It has shaped a skepticism that my generation, hidden from sight between the war of the millennials and boomers, holds pretty dearly. That skepticism is what keeps us from entering the war, and it is not lost on me that invoking the idea of generations is, in principle, somehow oxymoronic or just moronic and pitiable. Guilty. Don’t blame me; I need to think in shorthand to process this dog-and-pony shitshow; at least it’s not emojis.

I might suggest that this moment caught a beautiful, somewhat prismatic, colorful light, in which all the confounding history of the country and the world was being compounded before never-ending war, and larceny became the plat d’jour. It was also a time when letters were written, concerts were affordable, and it had not yet been entirely bitten by the vacuous service of identity politics. Everything would be decay; who fucking cares where Doris hides the pearls anyways? Of course, that also speaks to the privilege of the times, of being able to say fuck it ad nauseum.

Back to the artwork of Raymond Pettibon. Once I connected the dots between the album covers and learned what his brother did, Pettibon became an interesting icon of artmaking for me. I would not have guessed that his work would lead to where it has. Not that I don’t think it deserves it; it is just somewhat surprising to see it heralded by blue-chip galleries and on a Foo Fighters cover (Yes, I listened to Scream and Inside Out and understand the connections). Anything good from the underground is doubtless to see this type of exposure if left in the sun long enough.

With this, however contradictory in my mind, I realize that Raymond’s effect on the culture is probably better-known than other artists from his generation, like Julian Schnabel or Richard Prince (huge fan), only to be eclipsed, if I were to guess, by the influence of Basquiat, however badly that appears to be going at present.  His distribution system was youth-driven, not art-world booms and busts; thus, the kids who grew up with him understand his influence as tied to anti-establishment rhetoric, and his reach is more pervasive than that of the art-world heads mentioned for this reason. Seeing the art world establishment embrace the work feels in line with high fashion embracing Kim Gordon. It sits at cool, but has a slightly wobbly leg; might even be diabetic by now.

What I can say with this new book of his record covers, Nervous Breakdown: Raymond Pettibon: Album Covers, published by David Zwirner Books, is that I have come full circle to lick the dirty boot of this synthesis between outsider and insider, predominantly as it is hard to ignore the magnitude of such a project of collecting and exhibiting the ephemera and original work of Pettibon, by collector Stefan Thull at the WIlhelm-Hack Museum. It is a beautifully haggard opus of one man’s didactic embrace of American culture in these vital times, and a reminder of youth, skepticism, and the possibility of confrontation. Despite its lavishness, this is a firm reminder that an artist’s vision can continually challenge the monolithic presentation of subjects such as America, exposing its vast insecurities and problems while also paying homage to it. I mean, if it were not flawed, would it be entitled to such dialogue? The catalog, for people such as myself, has a bit of nostalgia attached to it, but in that nostalgia is a central theme of artists like Pettibon: defiance and the questioning of the established order, something that we seem to have forgone for the sake of expedited delivery and work-from-home shades of antidepressants.

 

No doubt, the Pettibon heads will enjoy this book, but I think if you are a music fan or were around between 86-96, you will recognize some of the golden honey of it all within. It is easy to get caught up in, and, as a record of one of America’s least conventional contemporary artists, it reveals the essential nature of escaping the art world and entering the cultural world of production. I could not recommend it more. If anyone were to escape into the world of contemporary art with an axe, I am forever entertained by, and happy that it has been, Raymond Pettibon, an artist so under-the-skin that it bears substantial remark about whether or not the audiences he oscillates between fully understand the power of his movements and work. Highly Recommended.

Raymond Pettibon

Nervous Breakdown: Album Covers

David Zwirner Books

items.title: Irina Rozovsky Mountain Black Heart
items.content:
The Balkans are very hard to describe. Though I have spent an inordinate amount of time in Greece, mostly in its capital, having traveled through the Balkans to get there, I remember a sense of something enigmatic, misty, and compelling as we traveled to and from Greece. I remember thinking about it all on a return stuck at the Serbian/Hungarian border for what seemed like an eternity, cars slowly inching forward, Orban’s deliberately difficult policy toward refugees causing innumerable delays and aggravations at checkpoints. Staying for a moment in Belgrade, I remember feeling that it was a world in which history felt explicitly jammed like ammunition in a chamber. On one hand, I had just passed the vestigial tail of a pro-Russian parade in the city as I was out shooting, and on the way out of town, we passed the Genex Towers, and I remember concrete bearing the marks of stray bullets from the 90s. I remember the Yugoslav Ministry of Defense building, a bombed-out husk, left to showcase wounds from the Allied NATO bombing of 1999, itself a reminder of the terrible atrocities of the Balkan Wars, something I would learn more about later through photographers such as Giles Peress, Robin Graubard, Nikos Economopoulos, Thomas Dworzak, and others.

When I learned about this stretch of Europe, I was taken aback. It felt so European, yet there was something slightly off-kilter in the air. It felt like a secret, or a promise. I could imagine all the horrors of lattes and chain malls eventually infiltrating Macedonia and Albania, being turned into a luxury waterfront, a theme that seems concurrent with attitudes in the present day. When I mentioned that it seemed like a secret, I could see so many possibilities for this place in Europe, but realized that opening up to the EU would also kill off what charm, however enigmatic it seemed, it held. Doubtless, if we do not blow ourselves up before long, we will see a transformation in Albania, Serbia, and perhaps the other countries.

When you read about Tito and his legacy, depending on the perspectives you encounter, you begin to understand the hardline regime, how it kept Yugoslavia intact for many years, but ultimately, how resilient its people have been over time. The complexity of its different identities presents a very coarse way to read its political situations, but one that does affect the various countries’ hostilities and camaraderie. To suggest that it takes an insider to understand these positions is not lost on me, particularly given the complexities and the discourses surrounding the upheaval of the 90s. Living in a former Soviet state, I can understand this to some extent, but I am careful not to assume that the Balkans can be symbolically linked to each of its parts.

For example, spending so much time in Greece, I came to the conclusion at some point about Greek identity, which often gets overshadowed by the diaspora effect of “we Greeks” when in reality, Greek identity is not as linked, despite what Christopher Nolan’s detractors may tell you, to its ancient past, though that is part of it. Instead, it is Balkan, a strange mix of Ottoman ancestry, European identity, and the Greek side of its nature. It has seen civil wars, been overrun by the CIA, been forced to be understood through its shipping history, and yet, like many countries, it has divisions in its provinces, islands, and broader areas that keep differences prominent. If you ask someone from Thessaloniki, or the Peloponeses, if they have much in common with Athens, of course, they will suggest the We Greek, but when you get into it, there are differences in each characteristic. If you take this example of Greece and magnify it x 1000, you might approximate the attitude of it within the framework of the Balkans, and yet, Greece itself rarely qualifies itself within that specific framework until you discuss Alexander the Great.

What strikes me as beautiful about the Balkans, from what little I have seen, is its sense of authenticity, something that is increasingly rare and diminishing in return. Perhaps this comes with a cost of non-participation, of wars almost starting over license plates and driving accidently ont he wrong trail, but ultimately, one gathers a sense of vitality, the essence of limited participation in a world spinning further out of control, a sense of being glued to the past, yet being able to recognize the flaws of the so-called future just outside one’s door. This authenticity is tied to the land, to the neighbors and enemies, and to the knowledge that a conflagration could easily begin just outside, on the road out of town, erupting into uncertainty and morbid prognostication. Or, it could usher in a new era of creature comforts, technology, data centers, and circumvented habit, a removal from what is known for what is promised as new and progressive. It is very hard to discuss what the Balkans will face in the coming years, but change is likely inevitable.

Irina Rozovsky’s Black Mountain Heart (MACK, 2026) examines the Balkans through two sets of eyes, though one set is inevitably American, the country where she lives. The other set of eyes is her background as a European, a Russian in fact. Though that was an early part of her life, it is an interesting question: how might her encounters have been facilitated, given the geography of her interests and her former country’s historically influential role in the region? In this, I am not positing a type of Euro-Gaze or Ameri-gaze, but thinking about how her wealth of lived experience has likely drawn her to this place rather than to a country like France, where she also spends a significant amount of time. I am curious how she relates to the 20th Century of our shared youth and how that influences this project filled with its chromophilic and flash tendencies, a Black Mountain sobriquet to nights passing into haloed days.

When I look at the book, I remember Dutch legend Bertien Van Manen’s A Hundred Summers, A Hundred Winters (1994), as well as East Wind, West Wind (2001). I am reminded of Van Manen when I think of Rozovsky’s color and her interest in portraiture, particularly the scarce indoor views found in the book. Something about the work speaks to a documentary practice, but it is not locked into the conditions or rules for which answers must be supplied. Instead, there is a stylization that borders on documentary tendency, but dissipates in the aggregate flow of images, in which not every image must give way to a potential narrative or “recording”. Rozovsky’s use of saturated color and flash also destabilizes any need to see this work in strictly genre terms.

What I might mention is that it is a significant departure from In Plain Air (MACK, 2021) in that, whereas both books share geography as a strategy, In Plain Air worked a much smaller patch of Prospect Park in New York, and the color was graded with type of halcyon sepia that gave the impression of cinema, a filmic potential that is not, by proxy found in the new book, which depending on what you find interesting in Irina’s work speaks to her flexibility as an artist working in color photography. I find both strategies equally engaging, but I read them slightly differently, with Mountain Black Heart arguably showing her versatility more than In Plain Air, in which everything congeals through the use of color grading and the uniformity of place. No doubt, this project feels slightly more serious in scope, and that is not to diminish from In Plain Air, which I thoroughly enjoyed, but here, there is a slightly more robust quality to the project and it feels, also by proxy of travel and movement to be the slightly more significant of the two and does indeed step into the realm of artists like Van Manen, mature and fully exhibiting what Rozovsky is capable of.

 

Irina Rozovsky

Mountain Black Heart

MACK

items.title: Kris Lüdi Smoke
items.content:
Toxic typology or cultural analysis of Swiss Agro-society, you be the judges. Either way, these little uns gunna smoke these here heaters until the cows come home. There is an amazing history of smoking in photography that Lucy Sante first cottoned onto sometime in the early 2000s with her book No Smoking. Several other smoking books have appeared since, most notably Ed Templeton’s Teenage Smokers and Thomas Sauvins Until Death Do Us Part, each outlining the cherished traditions of smoking in America and China. I won’t lie, I love smoking. I don’t do it as often as I should. Given the world that we live in, bordering on a technological and genocidal landscape, I find the act of smoking a bit of an act of defiance, the way it should be. I mean, everything is pretty much surveilled, we are cultivated not for our abilities in the humanities, or our creative endeavors, but for some mysterious and imagined idea of ecopnomy where we can be taxed to death with a an average lifespan indicating how much capitalism can extract from us, so why not, if were going down with the zhip at least make it expensive for them to keep our worker bodies in the shape necessary to produce and put a strain on their health services where applicable.

Smoking is indeed terrible for you, but think of how many people I have not killed when I smoked? I do believe there was a correlation in my youth where smoking actually gave me the peace I needed from reaching out to strangle someone. Instead of seeing smoking as a prelude to prison, see it as a prophylactic against homicide- a veritable cockblock to killing. Since becoming a father, my deepest regret is that I shield my kid from my habits and only smoke while on the road, which is infrequent at best. Fuck it, light em’ if you got ’em’. Let that secondhand smoke worm its way into untold lungs, cast a thick grey-veiled net across the sky, knock off part of the mosquito population if we’re lucky, I mean, what do those losers even contribute to the world, anyways?

 

The right to smoke, the need to smoke, the urge to NOT kill should be celebrated more widely. Why should we be shocked about how our society understands its relationship to nicotine anyway, when we’re tethered, manacled even to social media, 24-hour newscycles, and a blistering myopia that disincentivizes original thinking for influencer dividends, paid out in broad measure to some faceless cracker sitting atop the food chain. Is that a Chesterfield? I sit here with egg on my face. The Gordian knot of homeopathy and vagina-scented candles ruining the long-distance sight of my third eye, a useless tricyclops held hostage to some new fad, some craze for a modern kitchen filled with tasteless garbage passing itself off as the greens. Fuck you, and fuck your turnip-cinnamon baked potato crisps.

Kris Lüdi’s Smoke (Edition Patrick Frey, 2026) follows the annual tradition of cow judging in the beautiful alpine villages of Switzerland. Ahh, to be born Swiss, Jackpot. The book follows the children of the Appenzell villages as they smoke their way around the festivals that honor animal husbandry and agriculture. Permission is granted for this event, as it signifies the deep, personal relationship the communities have with the land and their livestock. It is a signal (smoke) of the country’s agricultural and tobacco production history, but also signifies an understanding that young people will inherit the future of local production through their labor. It is a custom that spans generations, and accepting the kids’ will to puff is part of the generational exchange between grandparents, parents, and the kids. Is it weird to look at? Fuck yea? Is it our place to judge local customs and cultural legacy? Hell no! I, for one, think that, given our concerns for children, we might need to worry more about those islands, files, pizzas, and gates than whether a kid wants to fire up a heater once a year while hanging out with his cow and family.

Throughout the book, Lüdi concentrates ont the faces of the kids. I am reminded of Jurgen Teller’s tight crops in Go See‘s and think the work overall is fun, and is slightly shocking until you get through the book once, then there is kind of a strange endearment that forms with the little bastards choking down a stogie and it makes me, above all, wanna slump against the barn wall with these little shits and talk about our woes over a coffin nail. I feel like we might get each other, might go something like this- “I gotta boil on my ass the size of Pittsburg, kid” “(but in German/French) “Don’t even get me started, old man, last week Billy stole my Pokémon cards and tried to give me a wedgie after gym class, before Urs kicked him in the sack for me in the locker room. He’s been pissing blood for a few days, but that’s his problem, shoulda never fucked with me“. At least that’s how it plays out in my head.

Overall, I think the book is really excellent. I like that it has a background to it and that it presents as a little bit shocking, but then I like how it settles in and I feel like I was born int he wrong country and that somehow this sort of cultural tradition might have decent side affects overall, keeping generations close, and refuting the modern obligation to see every fucking thing through the lens of social media, technology or money. There is something kind of fashion-like to it as well. Might be the point and shoot feeling of the images, can’t be sure, but no doubt this will be a classic down the road. Edition Patrick Frey is still kicking out awesome books. Get it!

 

Kris Lüdi

Smoke

items.title: John Gossage An Abridged Dictionary of Sculpture
items.content:
Sure, why not? Technically speaking, or at least relatively speaking, this is a kindly trove of American sculpture, itinerant in feel, something like an archaeological project that hints at Irving Penn, Avedon, and the side of Walker Evans people like to speak about ad infinitum as if we were all to marvel at the notion of tools separating us from the thumbless paws of beasts. Perhaps it goes beyond that to remark on the anonymous nature of shuttling back and forth to geographies of toil, distancing the body from its economic entrapment, if but for a fleeting moment, to be recognized, seen, and ultimately documented. But, within the realms of approximation, reasoning also suggests that it is kindly trove of shape, object, gravity, and weight culled from the celluloid tranche of one of the world’s greatest living sun-chainers. I am aware that my definition of what it could all be is veiled in an arrogant type of communication that belies either a serious form of pessimism or a relational digression toward the pretense of art. When in Marghera, eh?

An Abridged Dictionary of Sculpture (Steidl/The Agency, 2026) is a book of objects photographed by John Gossage over the years, placed on a white piece of paper, similarly to Avedon’s American West, or a 19th Century tuntype studio on wheels, pulling up to each town and in haste, placing a simple white backdrop against the rallying side of a barn to make pictures of the locals and possibly extract a tooth for an extra bit of shine. The white backdrop in this case becomes part of each image and is used rather brilliantly at times, with hands entering the side of the frame, with focal bleed as an object comes closer to the photographer, the focus otherwise thrown to the object further in the background. I believe a piece of white paper even makes the grade for some white-on-white crime. Many of the sculptures/objects from Arghera can be found in The Romance Industry, one of Gossage’s most significant titles from 2002, and it is, in my opinion, one of the finest books from his essential period. That work has several other chapters that elicit a sense of labor. One finds Gossage often reluctant to mention politics or ideology in his work, but when you kick a rock, it is pervasive: from Empire to There and Gone, even Map of Babylon deals with D.C. as a central cacophonous hub of political voices. His Berlin work is vital to this posture, and even his books Secrets of Real Estate and Nothing hint at capitalism, geopolitics, and ideology, respectively, even if he were to deny it.

This clever use of objects related to industry, its mechanical nature, and its byproduct made The Romance Industry something extraordinary, along with the more extensive imagery from Italy (and perhaps other climes). With its placement in this book, and its extended series of similar pictures from a broader series of locations and subjects, the book is asking the viewer to understand the itinerant study of objects as something less related to labor and politics, and more related to art, a motivation that is ever-present in many of Goassage’s books. Often, if you follow along, mentions of Cy Twombly, Jasper Johns, and his immense book collection all refer to a relationship with painting and sculpture that is as in-depth as it is in photography. In fact, his recent exhibition at Large Glass Gallery in London, John Gossage: From the Garden to the Darkness, 14 Mar —29 May 2026, had several works from his book Who Do You Love, which also use what he refers to as “elements”, pieces of paper, affixed to the mount in which his photographs appear, the result being something vaguelly collage-like and evoking a deep affinity to painting. I wonder if John ever dared to wield a brush, given. I present this as I think it’s fair to suggest there is a sympathy behind what I observe as political motivation in his work, and the pure desire to allude to other artists’ mediums. Does it preen a bit in such a blatant address? I will admit it does, but not enough to take away from the pictures.

Gossage is also a bookmaker with a very interesting use of graphic design, which I often feel harkens back to the 1930s. I am thinking of Bauhaus book design, particularly the use of multicolored bars illuminating numeration and type, similar to the work of László Moholy-Nagy, Jan Tschichold, and others. There is an interesting use by Gossage to illuminate the page with a type of concrete adornment in these highlights, as well as offsetting his images against a soft yellow paper background, which he has followed in many projects over the last 30 years, with There and Gone (1997) being a prime early example. This choice to relieve his photographic image from the page again suggests that we see the photograph in the book slightly differently than we do ont the wall. In the book, it can interact with the book’s layout and physicality differently than when presented in frames, elements aside. Gossage is a strangely great designer, though he gets there by being unconventional, and I am positive he designs for other artists and photographers, not for designers, who I am sure find his choices amateurish ont the surface, not understanding exactly how it activates the photography if they are not deep into the culture of photobooks. I do not always find the choices enabling, but historically, it ties John’s later books together in an interesting and identifiable way. So much so that seeing it applied to Raymond Meeks’ new book has been one of shared identity, but more on that later.

All in, I think this is a good Gossage title, but I wish, for his legacy and audience, that he had tried to find a way to reprint The Romance Industry under this title. Perhaps it is too complicated. Perhaps Nazraeli wishes to do so later. I do not know. If you have not seen that book, this is a nice indicator. If you have that book, as I do, this feels slightly less, by comparison, and the unison of images, though implicit in the dictionary (without description), doesn’t expand much on what that chapter in The Romance Industry already accomplished, but with better printing, of course. I have no idea what is up with Steidl. This is allegedly one of three new books produced by The Agency and Steidl, of the eighteen new titles I have read about. Let’s see what happens. I would not be surprised if we see 15 other titles under the Agency/Little Steidl imprint. Either way, this work comes from Gossage’s fecund period of production, so it is worth picking up for fans or those who never got a chance to see The Romance Industry. I find it a little glib, but for the most part, there are only lesser or better great Gossage books out there, so the juice is definitely worth the squeeze.

John Gossage

An Abridged Dictionary of Sculpture

The Agency/Steidl

items.title: Ying Ang Fruiting Bodies
items.content:
Mycellium and fungus in general have been a renewed interest as of late. Some of this is undoubtedly narrowed or zoomed in by the current fear of ecocide most of us are experiencing as we watch wildfires decimate geographies familiar and unfamiliar, as we are forced to watch data centers spring up around natural aquifiers- “If you have a milkshake, and I have a milkshake, and I have a straw… my straw reaches acroooooooss the room and starts to drink your milkshake. I drink your milkshake! I drink it up!”

Robert Macfarlane’s Underland: A Deep Time Journey from 2019 also examines the life underneath our feet, the largest living organic carpet in the world, while doing so with a poignant urgency. Merlin Sheldrake’s Entangled Life: How Fungi Make Our Worlds, Change Our Minds, and Shape Our Futures reaches similar conclusions about the unacknowledged land of the topic.

With all of this in mind, it is no wonder that artists such as Ron Jude, Ying And, Jason Fulford, and Heidi Sprecker have all found aesthetic value in the topic. With these artists, there is less of a lean toward the metaphoric potential of the mushroom, instead looking after the organism with a kind of sculptural awareness, with overtones of speaking about the fungi as if they were part of a separate taxonomy from that of human beings, and yet, there are some shared possibilities for using the fungi as a way to speak on several bodily manifestations of their being with our own.

Processed with VSCO with b1 preset

In Ying Ang’s (Perimeter, 2025) beautiful book of fungi, the metaphor suggests that the lifespan of fungi is similar to that of women’s reproductive lifespan. Ecologically inherent, the book offers a sublime look at sporocarps, or Fruiting Bodies, organisms whose main function is to reproduce and perpetuate the species. Fruiting Bodies are the above-ground and visible part of the mycelium, whose vast unseen network lies below the ground. Fruiting Bodies carry the metaphor of the female cycle by examining elements of the larger mycelial colony as they come to bloom, exhibiting their reproductive moment before shriveling, recoiling, and eventually shrinking into nothingness. There is something beautiful and deathly to the work, and it is fully engaging, with many images that almost suggest a natural history book or guide. But given the magnitude of the imagery, the fungi become very dominant on the page, exacerbated by lush color offset by monochrome interludes.

In looking at the book, without much foreknowledge or comprehensive reading, I found a synopsis of Katheryn Harlan’s book Fruiting Bodies: Stories that felt like an apt companion, or vice versa, for Ang’s book. The synopsis Fruiting Bodies ranges confidently from the fantastical to the gothic to the uncanny as it follows characters—mostly queer, mostly women—on the precipice of change. Echoes of timeless myth and folklore reverberate through urgent narratives of discovery, appetite, and coming-of-age in a time of crisis, and feel like a sympathetic fit to the work in Ang’s book.

With this in mind, I also find the world created in images hypnotic and enduring. Though there are focal metaphors to employ, I think the long line of textbook images from science class makes equal sense within the context of the work. I am drawn back to middle school, watching a nostalgic flip of the slide carousel, looking at my biology book, contemplating scribbling in marginalia for future generations of kids who might find my apocryphal notes littered on the pages alongside cordycepts, fngi, and these elegant fruiting bodies. Color photography can often evoke a strange, nostalgic feeling. I get the same distinctive emotion, a recall to memory when I look at color postcards from the mid-20th Century. It is uncanny, but dreamy in a pleasant way, technicolor, with deep, profound reds beating under the thumb, similarly to Ang’s use of red, which indicates everything from placenta to menses.

It has taken me a little time to wrap my head around the book, and I suggest that one does not need to see the symbolic overtures to enjoy it. It is, on its face, excessively beautiful, with an urgent ecology playing at its core, but when you add the engendered insight, it becomes visceral, something unintentional at first glance, but essential on the whole. I might also mention that I think the Perimeter team and the printer Wilco did a wonderful job of bringing the book to life. Narelle Brewer’s elegant design with the Perimeter team adds a concise weight to the work and never strays into the sad territory of overdesign that many photobooks wander into these days. Highly recommended

Ying Ang

Fruiting Bodies

Perimeter Editions

items.title: Anders Petersen Early Portraits
items.content:
In these days of irreversible rancor and decimation, one cannot help but look backward through the lens of a type in fogged nostalgia for the second half of the Twentieth Century, in the years prior to 2001, also embedded fairly as a time of grave uncertainty. Notwithstanding, this was a time when the travails of life under thumb were not constantly held up to one’s face 200 times a day, when the acrimony of the times was embedded in the nastiness of what came before, not what one currently experiences. Horror, atrocity, and decline are all very close today, and perhaps I am misremembering the horrors of those times, the Cold War, the nuclear rush, and unemployment. I was only there for the second half of the second half of that lean and mean century, where all the grain and violence that currently concerns our days was fomented and streamlined.

I think about the Twentieth Century often, having spent half of my life there. I look at the post-war condition of Europe, from where I have lived this half of my life, still deeply American, and wonder how such poor choices could be spread out on the baking sheet of political history, as rotted dough waiting to rise and envelop before its edges burn. I misguide my elegy for the times with music, with bohemian ideas of artistry, of times just before the wall fell, of dirty, crotchety, septic spaces where people would smoke indoors, cackle, and cavort without care, concern, or coercion of their identity by their handheld devices.

Where the reek of polyester and leather jackets comingled with hair spray and halitosis. Where Fassbinder was king, and Hasslehoff had not yet entered into consciousness. Where the RAF and the Munich Olympics were topical, but could be turned off. Where Aldo Moro might be mistaken as a dog food company, for the few people who had dogs as pets, believing them not to be itty-bitty schmoozy-woozy children, but to be custodial floor sweepers, an absorbant for everything that oen could not say to their kids or spuse while puttering in the garage or, more preceisely the cellar workspace, grasy fingers running along weathered linoleum countertops trying to grab a nail with dimionished eyesight in a land in which contacts had not yet been invented for the poor.

The tubercular smell of stale cigarette smoke, no filter, oozing from the bowels of the apartment complex, still riddled, pockmarked with bullet marks, and fading advertisements painted on ascending brick, below, a lot overgrown with weeds and shit emptying out its bowels of trash onto the cobbled streerts, humped rags and blankets in lying in a mound toward the back perhaps concealing living tissue, perhaps not, a veritble necrosis of sorts. Now rebuilt into custom flats for digital nomads working for Google, obsessed with vegan diets, their schmoozy-woozy animal children, and their declining birth rates.

When I look through Early Portraits by Anders Petersen, just as I do when I look through Novemberrejse, by Krass Clement, I am reminded of the twentieth Century and all of the mood and atmosphere, anxiety, and solitary time we had as human beings on the earth, with no tether to the digital 24 hour news cycle, perhaps a phone call here and there, but ultimately knowing where to be and when, with the option of disappearing whenever the call urged. The molasses of memory, impolite and untrustworthy as it can be, calls out in these pictures. As mentioned previously, I can almost smell them.

The grainy, haunting portraits produced by Anders Petersen shape how I interpret his world. I find his ability to project himself onto another person fascinating. There is a respectful distance in most of the photographs, and yet they are so concise and consistent that it is hard ot see them as anything other than a projection of the artist himself. They exude such subjective character that it would be nearly impossible to imagine them being from someone else. In some ways, I could make the bridge to Clements, as mentioned previously, and it would be fair to mention the long reach of Christer Strömholm, a known forebearer, associate, and someone potentially responsible for Petersen’s images from Clichy within the book. From that point on, it becomes harder to find a cult of references suitable for the work.

Throughout this volume of Petersen’s work, one can find their way around his Cafe Lehmitz moment, but outside of a few obvious references, the images used exceed the obvious, and the book, published by the eminent publisher Journal out of Sweden, uses images that are potentially less familiar to the audience for the most part. Whereas my history with Petersen is confined to Cafe Lehmitz, the book expands the territory and gives me something to grab onto beyond that spectacularly well-known volume. My world regarding the impresario is gravely expanded, and though I do not have his other volumes, I feel this is an exceptional tome of portraiture. I would suggest that people who are familiar with his work may still find something within, as the book flows incredibly well, being made of pieces from his different bodies of work, again showing the consistency of his production. I do not expect less from the Journal, Highly Recommended.

 

Anders Petersen

Early Portraits

Journal

items.title: Alvaro Deprit An Anatomy of Fear
items.content:
Art School is a process. It is one of those experiences in life that feels uncertain, tempting, and usually administered to those who wander, who are trying to fidn their footing in life, unashamed to be creative, yet unaware of what it will take to make a career in the arts feasible should they continue. There is a sense of experimentation and camaraderie in the halls where strange smells of hot glue and linseed oil mix and coagulate the nostrils, creating an ad hoc nostrum of familiarity and possibility. An occasional mature student gives advice, and a precocious youngster with parents who own a preposterous and expensive Thomas Houseago gleams from under sagging eyelids, not without talent, but locked in the trunk of their parents’ expectations, fraternizes with plaster of Paris, cocaine, and a deep-seated realization that they have a decade, if they stretch it, before they are recalled home to the family business.

The sounds include the soft hum of a kiln, to the screech of a saw on metal, cutting 90-degree angles, to be welded back shut. A teacher, whose career has involved making unfathomable yard sculptures/public art, plays the negative reinforcer, a slight trouser minnow erection dawning in his pants when he can make a student cry, giving ammunition to his next commission, a slight rub of that incongruent trouser on some unsuspecting student like a bad dentistry experience. Life continues this way, and before one knows it, they are cast out into the world of barristas if they are lower or middle class, and into real estate if they were lucky enough to be the sperm that won in a wealthy family. Lives will cross ever briefly, a congratulatory back pat for the most inconsequential of award trips through America with a Fulbright to boot. Eventually, the cloud of creativity dissipates with the pressures of the real world, and all but a few will continue onward as educators, festival organizers, and rarely, with a group show spot at a blue-chip gallery. That is part of the art school.

The other experience of art school is the proximity that one gains by being alive and allowed to understand the material world and one’s place in it through the experimentation of creation. Whereas I might have painted a dark view of the world above, one should understand that there is a reality to art practice and it is one of the greatest things one can do for themselves, but is also encumbered with maddening moments of trying to understand how to function in a world that does not value or appreciate art as a majority idea, but rather sees it not as a way of life and coping with the world, but as entertainment. Art is not entertainment for the artist, but rather an inexplicable feeling of highs and lows, of grounding one’s reality in an unrelinquishing world. It would not be remiss of me to say that it is essential, and for some of us, the only way we know how to make our way in the unrelenting world as we know it, using it to defy the expectations that have been placed on our imaginations, defying the normalization of standard work practice, and denying the outcomes of a society that rewards conformity over otherness. Without it, many of us would lose track of our essence, self-castigate our very beings for the sake of a birth-to-death lifespan in which nothing is gained, and freedoms are instead denied for the sake of the rapacious order of greed, of self-preservation, and of ugliness.

Alvaro Deprit’s book The Anatomy of Fear (Witty Books) looks at art school through its creations. It is a multi-generational story that uses the process of sculpture and half-made faces hidden and choking under layers of plastic as a metaphorical conversation about the anxiety of art schools and the interim timelines they represent to so many of those kids who grew up wanting to create, to be, and to be left with their thoughts, something that contemporary society does not reward, let alone encourage. This, of course, works itself out in the frenetic life of the student, with all those uncertainties I mentioned. As it is an abstraction to think through, using the busts hidden under plastic, to keep the clay from hardening, seems like an interesting enough metaphor to make the work hold ground. In fact, I was not aware that this was part of the project when receiving the book, and I found it an additional add-on that makes enough sense, but in reality, coming from such an environment and where I studied early on as a sculptor, I instead understand the impetus as one of process. I remember that smell of clay, or spraying it down after a day of work, before putting it under plastic to keep it from hardening at the edges, with a fondness. Granted, there was always something morbid about this process, especially after the bust began to take on a realism that gave one pause. Eye sockets and mouth cavities become sucked in, a strangulation victim looking for air, or a ghostly visit from a deceased relative that you thought you saw move from the corner of your eye before you, the last to leave, turned the lights off for the evening.

What Deprit’s work speaks to is anxiety, but also horror, within the uncanny sculptures’ underwraps. Their Munch-ian screams are silent, yet pleading for us to listen. An errant eyeball rolls down the corridor, and the calipers lie on dusty tables, suited for hanging one up by the ears as they are to measure anything. In essence, I think of this book less as a book about Gen Z and their problems with the world than as a strong horror novel. I see the work as emanating from the same haunted void as Medardo Rosso, and though I get that funding requirements might need a little metaphorical value, I specifically think it’s a great book on backroom sculpture and uncanny dopelgangers screaming back at us from the void of their creation, lockstep with our own contemporary horror of watching genocide and an onsalught of technological “progress” taking over our lives. It might be an anathema for people to consider getting right with clay, digging their hands into the dirt, and looking at the world through its material essence, not its digital imprint, but perhaps we might try. Again, I value this book for what I see directly and think it, as Alec Soth’s more recent Advice for Young Artists (cringe title) or Matthew Finn’s School of Art books will fit in the orbit of this. For those interested in the synthesis of sculpture and photography, and in the work of Brancusi, Rosso, or Rodin, I think this adds another layer to that tradition. Recommended.

Alvaro Deprit

An Anatomy of Fear

Witty Books

items.title: Victor Man: The Absence That We Are
items.content:
Victor Man’s painting presents a miasmic world in which death is presided over by the elegant souls of the living, and the living, in turn, are reminded of their duty as constant eulogizers of what has been lost. Playing technically off a nod to the kitsch black velvet paintings of the 1960s and to the brushstrokes of Gaugin and Van Gogh, Man’s nocturnal blue images, bathed in blue moonlight, evoke a number of art historical references from the preparatory paintings of morgue studies by Théodore Géricault for what would become one of the world’s greatest history paintings, The Raft of the Medusa to the unnatural colors of the Fauvists if they had been interested in the compositions of the northern renaiisance painting of Dieric Bouts or Rogier van der Weyden.

Victor Man

Pietas (Flower of Gaza), 2025 (Top), Oil on Canvas, 40 × 50 cm.

Ladro Dormente, 2024 (Bottom) Oil on Canvas, 11 3/4 x 15 3/4 inches (30 x 40 cm)

Oil on canvas

Further, his palette when considering the flesh of his subjects bears the necrotic color of Géricault’s mortuary limbs, while also asking the viewer to remember Grünewald ‘s specific choice of greeish-hued patina for the dead, deposed dried body of Christ found in the Isenheim altarpiece, a morbid icon representative of the subject matter, but also of the times in which it was painted, with a clear nod to the pestilence that lived in common memory from only a short time previous when Bubonic plague decimated Europe, taking up to one third of its population. In our contemporary moment, a distant echo, a morbid glossolalia, reaches our ears, reverberating like a worn church bell during our own flirt with the gangrenous possibility of plague in the early part of this decade. These paintings also remind me of Van Gogh and Gauguin, but I am possibly drawing that comparison from how I read the paint strokes of these recumbent, deathly faces.

 

Victor Man

Umbra Vitae, 2024-2025

Oil on canvas

10 5/8 x 13 1/8 inches (27 x 33.3 cm)

Framed: 17 1/8 x 19 3/4 inches (43.6 x 50 cm)

 

Further insinuations are the strange grotesques that sometimes infiltrate Man’s paintings, having wandered from their nest in the Prado museum, leaving the edge of Bosch’s ethereal painting, to find themselves nestling in the back of Man’s paintings, conveyed like a sucker punch to the back of the neck, where they invoke an otherworldly insistence to be understood as hellish amongst the mourning tears. These elements are scarce, but when they do appear, they suggest an affinity to the absurdity of casualty in the mind of the living, echoing a time in which painting, outside of Odd Nerdrum, was still invested in ethereal suggestion within the plausible realms of a stilted realism.

Victor Man

Maternity (Curve Delle Anime), 2025

Oil on canvas

31 7/8 x 25 5/8 inches (92 x 73 cm)

In more recent developments in painting and drawing, I am reminded of Steven Shearer to some extent, though the color scheme and subject matter are scattershot. I cannot exactly pinpoint it, but I understand the two artists as living in the same universe, if on slightly different continents. Both artists faintly echo the esoteric tendencies of the symbolists and painters like Gabriel von Max, who are also not lodged in a distant orbit.

Victor Man

Maternity with Legend, 2024

Oil on canvas

36 1/4 x 28 3/4 inches (92 x 73 cm)

A recluse of sorts, Man’s work has found a home both with the Gladstone Gallery and more recently and in the subject of this article with David Zwirner. One can assume a deep affinity to the work when the gallery owner writes the preface for the book of images. As a first catalog, I find it refreshing that the work has been photographed in situ and that it presents a sense of scale for those unable to attend the exhibition. The paintings are not overly large, which is refreshing in a day when post-war upscale makes intimacy feel slightly alien. I also like the notion that Man and Zwirner’s experience in his studio is somewhat clandestine in an age where the artstar is finally in decline. The humility of getting on with it, making work, and becoming unfettered with Frieze celebrity suggests a reshuffling of focus to the work, not the ego.

Victor Man

Maiden with Skull, 2024

Oil on canvas

31 7/8 x 25 5/8 inches (81 x 65 cm)

As for the book itself, it is well-designed, compact, and to the point, which gives Man’s work the space to inform. With this in mind, I would highly recommend those interested in painting to pick this up as we turn the bend from work informed by our desire to speak through technological means to work that is representative of what human creativity can produce by hand, and to produce it without being mired in the conventions of post-modern abstraction and digression. As someone who writes from outside of the realms of painterly knowledge, and as a proponent for photographic culture, this work has struck a nerve with me in that it feels relatable to the condition of the 21st Century, its genocidal impulse, and its tremendously dire circumstances that most people find themselves in, alienated from the body, the mind, and each other. What else have we but lament and toil? Highly Recommended.

Victor Man

Gypsy Girl with Apparition, 2025

Oil on wood panel

15 3/4 x 11 3/4 inches (40 x 30 cm)

Victor Man

The Absence That We Are

David Zwirner Books

items.title: Hujar: Contact
items.content:
This is the second book from MACK offering a look into the theme of contact sheets presented over the past year. The first was David Armstrong’s book Contacts (I mean, how else should you call these, Sheets?), published last October, which similarly examined a brilliant tranche of Armstrong’s work through the diminutive, if plentiful, images on his contact sheets. Both artists share some crossover in themes. Both Hujar and Armstrong are very talented portraitists and have captured that thin slice of bohemia mixed with notable fame found between Boston and New York. With Armstrong, his deep friendship with Nan Goldin is, and many of the other “Boston School” artists of the 70s and 80s brought him close to Hujar’s circle of similar associations in New York.

There is some extended overlap between the artists and their shared history of LGBTQ within the scene, also bringing their intentions closer into alignment, namely to document, as part of their practice, the men and women whose efforts at gay liberation are now considered historic. These two books are to be seen first as documents of the artist’s creative life and, second, as a form of historical archaeology. Both tomes outline the artist’s process through giving the viewer a more comprehensive look at the photographs/frames that were not chosen as part of the iconic output, giving the reader a broader sense of each artist’s approach to subject and camera, which may seem a bit inwardly geeky, but does not diminish from the subject matter itself.

With Hujar: Contact, the resounding experience of thumbing through the many photographic frames presented within is at once nostalgic for some of us who have followed Hujar’s work since the 90s or earlier, presenting iterative portraits of the key individuals that have aligned his career and life, sometimes associated to his exceptional book Portraits in Life and Death, from 1976,  these characters begin to emerge from the overflow of images and one, if familiar with that book begins to pose and trace circles over the faces of those subjects, looking at adjacent images, imagining how the book might have been different with a slightly different protrait at a different angle, realizing, for example, among other things, that there were actually very few images of the Palermo Capuchin Crypts, when perhaps one expected more, acknowledging Hujar’s deep skill in getting the images that he did in such a low-lit and existential environment ( I have photographed it several itmes, it is overpowering). Paul Thek becomes an essential character in the book, Hujar’s boyfriend and an eminent artist in his own right, and we trace the relationships, desires, and camaraderie throughout the book and the city itself.

There is a mix of squares and 35mm film, which is interesting as it takes a special type of mental gymnastics or rewinding each time the camera is changed on the book spreads. The format often dictates the image composition and how the operator, to a great extent, makes work, and in my estimation, it’s fairly clear that Hujar was very gifted with the square over the rectangle. It also appears to be his preference. The square, though it may sound contrary when written, is actually quite amenable to the idea of portraiture, for which Hujar was a master. One might think that a rectangle fits the human form better, but with skill in posing, the square becomes more intriguing for the choices that must be made in getting the subject within those walls successfully. It asks the photographer to bend the knee often and to get close to their chosen subject, creating intimacy. Many of Hujar’s greatest images come from his squared-off subjects, like Susan Sontag, Candy Darling, William Burroughs, etc., all recumbent, some lying down, others casually prostrate. It makes the frame feel tight but not claustrophobic, bringing the viewer very close to the subject without much distraction.

Queer and intellectual icons surface through the contact sheets. The pope of filth, John Waters, William S.Burroughs, Candy Darling, David Wojnarowicz, and more, and where this is an exceptional trove of material for that community, one only needs to skim the photographs inside to realize how essential his coverage of the New York scene in the 70s and 80s was. He caught the spark as it began to rage into a full-blown fire, capturing several generations of icons, many of whom would be lost like himself and Thek, much before their time. It is with some lament that we read these portraits, but greater still is the need to recognize their significance and Hujar’s great gifts and contributions, to see in all the boudoir application a life documented and lived as art, and artful with purpose.

Again, I feel the need to praise Mack’s courship of publishing archival material like this. It is manna for many of us who feel the photobook world at large is shrinking into redundancy, repetitiveness, and just general uninspired churning. These books offer a broader look at lives of significance and cross the thresholds of various cultural appetites, from LGBTQ studies to death studies to AIDS-related social studies to the procedural role of the photographic process. I find these mediations entirely successful. Although Hujar is having another moment, having been re-examined by MACK and Moyra Davies previously, alongside Primary Info’s excellent book on his relationship to Thek, I think this gives one of the more rounded visual assessments of his work as there is literally so much to see that one can inform oneself about the artist’s talents more than other catalogs from Mapfre, or monographs by Scalo, etc. There is no shortage of Hujar material out there, but this offers a more rounded context without laboring to be simply another survey. I really hope, between this and the Armstrong books, that we might see more and more of this type of archival digging. Highly Recommended.

Peter Hujar: Contacts

items.title: Nicola Buonomo Luoghi
items.content:
A field guide in parts, an attempt at shorthand analysis.

Places, not much else needs to be said when so much has already been said.

The strong presence of Guido Guidi, as if you were to take his large-format images of Cesena and use a 35mm camera to catch some of his shadow work.

A mix of formats: not only is there 35mm, but there is also a square 120 format in the book, which shows the artist’s comparative framing ability in both formats. Of course, this may have been from cropping, but I do not sense it.

A game of triangles and shadows, jagged keep of absences and presences, pervades the work. Sometimes all you need is a shadow to convince the frame to follow compositions that speak photographically, without the encumbrance of language. You can feel a shadow, revel in its cookie-cutter negative space, almost like a celluloid negative itself, challenging the notion of the double.

 

On the use of doubling. One scene, one position, shot over time, momentum builds, one forensically passes over the flattening of light through the passage of time. The differences are in the light itself, not the subject. This has been effectively used to explain the rational possibility that there are unlimited ways of understanding our time stretched out in our lives, while also courting the very insignificant presence that we inhabit as we toil, observe, and seek some understanding of the bigger questions of purposefulness, our utility to the geography and era we lumber and (sadly) slumber through. This doubling is an efficient mechanism for explaining photography’s position to time, light, and essence.

Contact posture. Throughout, there are uses of grids, both in small intervals and which build into almost achieving a full contact sheet, an analog resistance and medium-specific dialog from the artist to remind us of the alchemical nature of light and silver, to remind us of its haptic potential in an age when all is pixel. It makes, though not as a fundamental decree, the nature of engagement, for those trapped on the inside, reciprocity of nitrate and materiality. The black lines, scanned to show the frames’ void, are included and become part of the composition, creating an interesting game of lines and continuation. The desire to put full black frames around scanned negatives is always so very appealing, a question of structural suggestion and integrity, again, material.

On the X in photography, a recurring theme featured in works by John Gossage (Berlin), Joachim Schmidt (The Spot), Thomas Barrow (Cancellations), and, more recently, Odette England’s discussion on the matter. It is a historical annotation within and on top of frames that makes it intriguing for what it does and for what it purports to undo through its intersections. Within these places, it occurs several times, though softly, without the brash need to obfuscate entirely.

What I take away is a soft illuminating study of places, of shadows, and a hazy soft type of existential memorabilia in which my feet are blistered by sand, the buzz of cicadas land noisily in my ears, and the sun blinds me with a resistance to my being, but ultimately accepts there is work to be done that surpasses its very dominant nature toward something sublime, uplifting and tidal, an experience caused by its opposite, the lunar. There is a playfulness with the formats and sequence of the book, and I am unable and unwilling to leave the long reach of Master Guidi.

Where Buonomo succeeds is not simply looking like one of the master’s many imitators, but standing in his own orbit, looking for a way to expand and not contract that universe of Italian photography, for which I am exceedingly grateful, and there are simply too many imitators. Luoghi is within its own territory, within its own set of investigations, and nobody owns the shadow or sun, or the use of two frames, though others have tried to suggest as much and failed. What is developing here is a strong vision that I believe can be expanded on into something even more vital as time marches on. Rebar will fade to even more stone, telephone poles will opt out, and gardens will grow thicker, if anything is to continue to grow at all.

I highly recommend this book. It is a very strong offering for a young artist finding their voice within a strong genre of photography that we all painfully respect. I hope he continues with the framing, the shadow work, and continues to homage others, while not letting them in too close. Respectful distance is still respectful. Great stuff and a great addition to the Kult Books output, designed with clarity, light experimentation, and a great cover.

 

Nicola Buonomo

Luoghi

Kult Books

items.title: Stephanie Kiwitt Fortaufend
items.content:
The ideas of usefulness and aesthetic appearance often come into conflict over time in architecture. Decay, cracks, erosion, and palimpsests of change clash and defy our natural sense of wholeness when we look at buildings that have persisted over decades, if not centuries. I am thinking particularly of 19th and early 20th-century buildings, those that have not been applied for the historical blue plaque, graded and listed buildings that tourists occasionally spot, notified of it being the birthplace of a famous musician or writer, which, of course, is the majority of those buildings. Instead, these unremarked edifices are caught observing with their bizarre patchwork of cement repairs, their dangling ganglia of wiring hanging from odd angles, and their strange mismatch of window casements that look out of place and forced into the original facade to ensure against the harsh climates of the present, yet look utterly and unapologetically out of place. Satellite dishes half haphazardly off of red brick, rusted, and out of use, but not to be removed from their perch on the side of the house. Rusted letterboxes hang casually to one side, creaking as owners check for bank notifications and the errant local pizza or kebab advertisement shoved callously inside the precarious object by some underpaid flyer-stuffing immigrant, with their time spent dodging dogs and the wrath of territorial owners.

These buildings are particularly noticeable along the former upkept utility of towns that once had thriving mines, row houses, now hidden under coagulated plaster and cement repairs were shelters for the coal-stricken miners and their families who used to bring prosperity to the region at grave personal imperilment, the threat of gaseous fumes rendering their bodies unconcious or worse, the dark fate of being left to die in a partially collapsed mine shaft. These homes, though simple, effectively gave laborers a place to sleep, smoke like chimneys, and raise generations of children desperate to avoid the same mines in which Papa lost his leg. These homes, and the civic building they were attached to, the bureaucracy hubs for social services, unemployment, and medical insurance, have been left vacant as the minbe’s refused to give, and these small flatland towns lost their original purpose or ability to hold inhabitants as children flee from rural boredom and factory work to urban centers and a chance at what was once considered prosperity, now limited by the progress of technology and the high costs associated with our new fifedom. The cities, paved with gold, dripping with honey, are no longer the make-it-until-you-break-it epicenters; instead, they have become an albatross, a playground for grifters and the wealthy.

 

With all of this aside, there have been accusations pointed in my direction of what has been called post-industrial gloaming, a way to see the de-industrialization in contemporary society as a type of ruin porn, a lament for toxicity and bad air, a lament for work, a lament for purpose, and a lament against technifeudalism and a championing of a form of aesthetic or subjective ludditism. Of course, I think that is a stretch, but I cannot help but feel part of an age in which these subjects matter, and they seem to matter further as we slide into the morass of joblessness, purposelessness, and uncertainty in the age of AI and robotics. What will we do with all of this -non-exertion? What will towns on the periphery do with themselves as the paint peels? Do we need more poets? Where does our toil meet our utility as a species? All of these questions persist when I look at Stephanie Kiwitt’s Forlaufend, published by Spector Books. This volume of hinterlands, passageways, crumbling brick, and architectural palimpsests reminds me of city-examiner Stephan Keppler in places, but overall, I am convinced by Kiwitt’s constant examination of these marginal post-industrial geographies that we are on the precipice of erasure of our humanity and our purpose. I do not qualify that as the intention of the work, but how I feel when I examine her observations of form, of trace, and of the ephemeral decline of working society through its architectural elements.

 

Most of the photographs in the book examine the Saxony-Anhalt region of Germany. It is a continuation of her Flächenland work in that it has become an encyclopedia of these areas, both cartographically/topographically, and now in part measured by the decision to photograph the elements, both sculptural and in detail, which changes the prescription from Flächenland somewhat, moving from color to black and white while also looking from a distance, to something more scrutinizing and up-close in this volume. I relish projects like this that are ongoing and dense. I can also suggest Aleix Plademunt’s recent survey Site (also SPector Books) as a project that feels in tune with this work, though the source material varies. These thick compendia of observation and associations present very compelling arguments for durational projects. I have been following Kiwitt since her Maj book, which I still see as brilliant and not that far removed from theoretical territory compared with Flächenland and Forlaufend. This volume presents a brilliant continuation, and the expansive use of work spread across multiple volumes is something I find fresh and offers an interesting turn in the artist’s work. You do not need both volumes per se, but it is a bit of a shame to understand one without the other. Go get it!

Stephanie Kiwitt
